21.0.big: Viruses aren't cells (they're acellular). They can only make copies of themselves inside a living host cell.
points: They infect every kind of life (bacteria, plants, animals) and cause diseases from colds to HIV. A virus that causes disease is a pathogen.

21.1.big: A virus is just genetic material (DNA or RNA) inside a protein coat. Scientists group viruses by how they make their mRNA.
points: Discovery: the porcelain filter removed bacteria, yet the filtered liquid still made tobacco plants sick, so something smaller was at work. Viruses were first seen with the electron microscope (1930s).

Where viruses came from is unclear. Devolution/regressive: they shrank down from free-living cells. Escapist/progressive: they're bits of DNA or RNA that escaped from cells. Self-replicating: they came first.

A virion is one virus particle outside a cell: a virus core (nucleic acid) inside a capsid made of capsomeres, sometimes wrapped in an envelope stolen from the host's membrane. Matrix proteins sit between capsid and envelope.
Viruses attach using viral receptors (often glycoproteins) that fit specific host molecules. That's why each virus infects only certain species and cells.
Positive polarity (+) RNA can be used directly as mRNA. Negative polarity (−) RNA has to be copied first.

Baltimore classification, 7 groups: I dsDNA (herpes), II ssDNA (parvovirus), III dsRNA (rotavirus), IV ss(+)RNA (cold, polio), V ss(−)RNA (rabies, flu, measles), VI ssRNA with reverse transcriptase (HIV), VII dsDNA with reverse transcriptase (hepatitis B).

21.2.big: Every virus follows the same basic steps: attach, get in, copy and assemble, get out.
points: Attachment: viral receptors bind to the host cell. The cell must be permissive (able to support the virus).
Entry: phages inject only their DNA. Animal and plant viruses come in by endocytosis, or by fusion of the envelope with the membrane (only enveloped viruses can fuse).
Replication and assembly: the host's machinery copies the viral genome and makes viral proteins. Retroviruses (HIV) use reverse transcriptase to turn their RNA into DNA.
Egress (exit): lysis (the cell bursts and dies) or budding (virions leave one at a time wrapped in membrane, so the cell may live a while).

Bacteriophages infect bacteria. Lytic cycle: take over, copy, burst. Lysogenic cycle: viral DNA hides in the host chromosome as a prophage and gets copied every time the cell divides. Stress can flip it into the lytic cycle.

Animal viruses can cause an acute disease (short), a chronic infection (long-lasting), or latency (hides, then comes back, like chickenpox returning as shingles). They're cytopathic when they damage cells. Oncogenic viruses (like HPV) can cause cancer.

Plant viruses spread by horizontal transmission (from outside, like insects) or vertical transmission (parent to offspring). Symptoms: hyperplasia (overgrowth, like galls), hypoplasia (stunting), cell necrosis (dead tissue), and discoloration (yellow spots).
21.2.tip: Lytic = loud (burst now). Lysogenic = lying low (hiding in the DNA).

21.3.big: Vaccines prevent viral disease by training your immune system ahead of time. Antiviral drugs slow viruses down but can't cure most infections.
points: Vaccines use weakened (attenuated) live viruses, killed viruses, or viral pieces. Rarely, a weakened virus can mutate back to the dangerous form (back mutation).
Antivirals block a step of the virus's life cycle. AZT blocks reverse transcriptase, so HIV can't make DNA from its RNA. Anti-retroviral cocktails hit several steps at once.
Viruses can be used for good: phage therapy kills antibiotic-resistant bacteria, oncolytic viruses attack cancer cells, and gene therapy uses viruses to deliver healthy genes.

21.4.big: Even simpler than viruses: prions are just misfolded proteins, and viroids are just naked RNA.
points: Prions have no DNA or RNA. A misfolded PrPsc protein makes normal PrPc proteins refold into the bad shape (extra pleated sheets), which piles up and destroys brain tissue.
Prion diseases: mad cow disease (BSE), kuru (spread by ritual cannibalism), and vCJD in humans. They can't be killed by normal sterilizing.
Viroids are tiny, single-stranded, circular RNA with no protein coat. They make no proteins and infect only plants (potatoes, tomatoes, avocados).

opts: DNA or RNA, though present, is not transmitted when a prion causes infection.
The prion does not contain any DNA or RNA.
Only parts of DNA or RNA are transmitted in a prion.
Far more protein than DNA or RNA is transmitted in a prion.

1.why: The filter removed bacteria, but the liquid still caused disease, so something smaller (a virus) was there.

2.why: Viruses are too small for light microscopes. The electron microscope showed them.

3.why: Devolution/regressive: viruses came from free-living cells that lost parts.

4.why: Viruses leave no fossils, so much is still unknown.

5.why: A single virus particle outside a cell is a virion.

6.why: Viruses latch on with viral receptors that fit molecules on the host.

7.why: Positive (+) RNA can be read directly as mRNA.

8.why: Rabies is a single-stranded (−) RNA virus (group V).

9.why: To see inside a virion, you need a transmission electron microscope. Scanning EM shows surfaces.

10.why: Viruses can change how the cell works or kill it.

11.why: In budding, virions leave one at a time, wrapped in host membrane.

13.why: Lytic makes new phages right away. Lysogenic first merges the phage DNA into the host genome.

14.why: False: fusion needs an envelope, so naked viruses can't use it.

16.why: Released virions go on to infect nearby cells and repeat the cycle.

17.why: HIV is a retrovirus: it must turn its RNA into DNA.

18.why: Herpes simplex causes skin lesions (like cold sores).

19.why: Measles starts with a runny nose and sore throat and can cause pneumonia: nose and lung infections.

20.why: Vaccines prepare the immune system to fight future infections.

21.why: Anti-retroviral drugs block steps of the virus's replication cycle.

22.why: Parotitis (swollen salivary glands) is caused by mumps.

23.why: PrPsc is the misfolded form. PrPc is the normal one.

24.why: Kuru spread person to person through ritual cannibalism in Papua New Guinea.

25.why: Viroids are single-stranded RNA with no protein coat.

27.why: Prions make normal proteins change shape into the misfolded form.

28.why: Even after filtering out bacteria, the liquid still infected healthy plants.

29.why: New technology (like DNA sequencing) gives scientists new kinds of information to test their hypotheses.

30.why: Viruses need a matching receptor. Measles can't attach to dog cells.

31.why: Viruses that make mRNA the same way behave similarly.

32.why: AZT blocks reverse transcriptase, so HIV can't make DNA from its RNA.

33.why: In the lysogenic cycle the viral genome is copied into every daughter cell. Each one can later go lytic, so in theory far more virions come out.

34.why: Shingles patients can spread the virus. Someone never exposed would get chickenpox first; shingles only comes later from latent virus.

35.why: If the virus can't attach, nothing else can happen.

36.why: Measles can cause encephalitis (brain swelling), which can be deadly.

37.why: Viroids have the tiniest genomes and the highest mutation rates. Tiny genome = extremely small particle.

38.why: On the graph, bigger genomes have lower mutation rates. A low rate for an ss(+)RNA virus suggests a genome above 10,000 nt (it's about 30,000).

39.why: vCJD spread through poorly sterilized surgical tools and pituitary growth hormone from infected cadavers.

40.why: A misfolded protein causing other proteins to misfold = prions.

41.why: Prions are just protein. They contain no DNA or RNA at all.

42.why: Group I is dsDNA, so RNA is made from a DNA genome. Group III is dsRNA, so RNA is made from an RNA genome.

43.why: Group I = DNA genome, transcribed to RNA. Group VI = RNA genome that must be turned into DNA by reverse transcriptase first.

44.why: At step 2 the viral RNA enters the nucleus and starts being copied, so the amount of viral genetic material starts to rise.

45.why: The precancer curve rises right after the HPV infection peak, so high infection leads to more precancerous growths. Cancer stays low.

46.why: In lysogeny, viral DNA is part of the host chromosome, so it's copied every time the cell divides.

47.why: False. Under bad conditions the prophage leaves the genome and goes lytic.
